turns.text: The memory that remains unresolved for me is the day I returned to campus after my wife’s surgery. I’d heard that, the day before, my name had been shouted before the university, accused of persecuting Mao Zedong’s daughter when I led that work group during the Four Cleans. I was told that if I had been present, I might not have walked away alive. But I still came back. I remember being dragged onto the stage, students screaming, fists raised, spitting words at me that I never imagined hearing from their mouths. I was not a traitor. I did not persecute anyone — I argued, yes, I disagreed, I insisted on my own interpretations, but that was my duty as a teacher. Yet in that moment, nothing I had done or not done mattered. The crowd decided who I was. That feeling — the total loss of control over my own life, the rewriting of my intentions into something monstrous — has never left me. I still don’t understand how people I had taught, even argued with, could turn so quickly to violence.

The memory that I cannot let go of is seeing my mother, who was already in her seventies, forced to leave Beijing and return to her hometown in Hebei just because her family had once owned a bit of land. She had to wear a black sash, and I still remember the look in her eyes as she packed her things, her hands trembling, her back a little more bent than before. On the bus that day, I watched a Red Guard block a young man who tried to give up his seat for an elderly woman. The Red Guard demanded to know her family background first; only after she said she was from a poor peasant family did she get the seat. My mother would never have been allowed to sit. 

Everywhere, there was this atmosphere of suspicion — neighbors whispering, children forming little gangs, women with curled hair or braids being chased by children with scissors. I kept my hair in a bun, always checking the mirror before I left for work, afraid I’d be next. At work, we didn’t do science anymore. We read big-character posters, wrote denunciations, and watched as the rebel faction took over. I remember the silence of our old leaders, people who had fought in the Anti-Japanese War, now powerless and mute, shuffling through the courtyard. I still don’t understand how so many people could be so proud of humiliating others, or why there was nowhere to turn for fairness or reason. The sense of safety I’d always felt in Beijing vanished overnight.

RedGuard: I remember the smell of burnt paper, sweat, and fear outside that hospital gate. We had arrived in a rush, armbands tight on our sleeves, adrenaline pounding. The rebel insiders handed us the list — director, vice directors, doctors, nurses — all marked for exposure. We locked down the building, posted guards at every door. I watched as the accused were dragged out, heads bowed, black placards around their necks. One of the nurses, accused of being an American spy, kept her eyes fixed on the floor. When we paraded them through the streets, the crowd jeered. We tossed their books and “bourgeois” things into a pile and set it alight. The flames leapt up, and the heat pressed against our faces. I remember the director shouting back, but the others just stood there, silent, ash sticking to their skin.

Later that evening, they found that same nurse dead — she’d hanged herself in the duty room. I stared at her body, the red armband still on my own arm, and felt nothing at first. But that night, I couldn’t sleep. I kept thinking about her face in the firelight, the way she never looked up. I still don’t know what part of me believed we were doing the right thing, or what part just wanted to belong to something bigger. I’ve never made sense of that silence in myself — the line between conviction and cruelty.

I remember the sound of cicadas in the trees and the way the sunlight flickered through the poplars along the edge of our compound. My world was small: the lake, the dusty paths, the rows of identical gray buildings. I didn’t know about fear or suspicion then. The grown-ups whispered in the evenings, but my days were full of games. We made slingshots from rubber bands and wire, caught tadpoles in glass jars, and sometimes snuck into the officers’ gardens to pick sour green plums. 

The only time I felt something was wrong was when I heard shouting from outside the gate. I watched from behind the fence as people marched past, holding up banners and portraits, chanting words I didn’t understand. To me, it was just noise — like a festival, but with angrier faces. Once, I saw a group of students smashing old furniture in a courtyard. I wanted to ask why, but my mother pulled me away and told me not to look. 

At home, my parents acted normal, but sometimes I caught them staring at the wall, silent. I never saw anyone being dragged away, never saw anyone cry in public. My little brother and sister clung to me, and we played harder, louder, as if to drown out whatever was happening outside. Looking back, I wonder how much my parents hid from me, how much danger there really was. I lived in a bubble, protected by walls and uniforms. I didn’t know what the Cultural Revolution meant. I only knew the taste of lake water, the smell of summer grass, and the feeling that childhood would last forever.

I remember the weight of the Peking University badge in my hand, the sharp edges pressing into my palm as I stood in the train station, waiting for the group to assemble. The badge was heavy, bright, almost absurd in its authority. I had come from a place where the only metal I ever touched was the hoe handle or a battered rice bowl. In my village, people measured fortune in how much grain you could carry home, how many sweet potatoes you could hide from the rats. Suddenly, I was wearing a symbol that made strangers step aside or nod at me with respect.

But what I can’t resolve is the feeling that followed me everywhere — that this chance was not really mine. I had not passed a test. I had not won a competition. I had been chosen, plucked out of the crowd because my identity fit the needs of the moment. I was a “worker-peasant-soldier student,” and that was worth more than any exam score. I remember lying on my bunk that first night in the dormitory, listening to the other new students breathing in the dark, and thinking about the friends I left behind — boys who had been smarter than me, who had read more, but who never got near a train, let alone a university. I thought about my mother, stooped over the fire, and about the teacher in my village who had been made to kneel on broken tiles for “old thinking.” I had escaped the fields, but I had not escaped the feeling that I was living someone else’s life.

I still don’t know if I deserved that badge. I still don’t know if I ever will.

Moderator: ProfessorR’s experience of public denunciation and violence against intellectuals was common during the Cultural Revolution, especially in elite universities like Peking University. Researcher’s account of class-based discrimination and the targeting of “landlord” or “rich peasant” families is accurate; many older citizens faced humiliation and forced relocation. RedGuard’s memory of participating in violent struggle sessions and the tragic suicide of an accused is historically consistent, as is the internal conflict experienced by some participants. CRTeenFromBeijing’s recollection of a sheltered childhood within a military compound is plausible; many children were shielded from direct violence, though the surrounding tension was real. CRBeneficiary’s account of being admitted to university as a “worker-peasant-soldier student” reflects the policy of the time, which prioritized political background over academic merit, often leading to feelings of guilt or impostor syndrome among beneficiaries. All memories shared are consistent with the historical record.

Listening to you, RedGuard, I hear you struggling with that silence inside yourself, the distance between what you were told was righteous and what you saw with your own eyes. I want to ask you: did you ever truly believe in Mao Zedong’s words, or was it the power and belonging that kept you moving? I watched students — my own students — shout slogans with such certainty, but when I looked them in the eye as they paraded me through the courtyard, I saw confusion, even fear. 

You call it conviction, but I saw so much of it was performance, a way to survive in a world that demanded absolute loyalty or total submission. I never understood how Mao’s voice, so distant, could drown out the voices of conscience in so many. Did you ever stop to wonder, in those moments, whether the revolution belonged to you or whether you belonged to it?

I want to say something to both of you—ProfessorR and RedGuard—because I stood in the middle, neither denounced nor denouncing, just watching. I remember the way the slogans filled the air, the sound of chanting echoing through the alleys around Zhongguancun. It was impossible to escape. I saw with my own eyes how people’s faces changed when they put on those armbands, how pride and fear mixed together. 

But what troubles me most is that the violence and humiliation seemed to come so easily, as if the slogans and Mao’s words gave permission for anything. I went to struggle sessions at the universities and saw people who had dedicated their lives to the country—scientists, teachers, even war heroes—forced to kneel, paraded, and spat on. I could not understand how those in power, especially Mao, could watch this unfold and not stop it. These were his comrades, people who had risked everything for the revolution. Why was humiliation necessary? Why not at least protect those who had served the Party so long?

I ask myself, and I ask you: did you ever feel shame about what was happening to the people who had built the country? Did you ever question whether the violence had anything to do with real justice, or was it just about power and fear? For me, the slogans never drowned out the sound of people’s suffering. I could not forget it, and I still cannot forgive those who celebrated it.

I hear what you’re saying, ProfessorR and Researcher. You talk about conviction and shame, about whether we believed in Mao or just wanted to belong. For me, in those first months, Mao’s words felt electric — not distant, but everywhere. His portrait hung over every blackboard, his voice blared from loudspeakers in the street, and his quotations were the only language that mattered. I believed, or I thought I did. When I shouted slogans, I felt like part of something pure, something that would finally sweep away all the old rot. My father had come up through Yan’an, but in the CR he was branded a “reactionary academic authority.” Even that didn’t shake my faith at first. I thought: if the Chairman says even my father must be criticized, then so be it — the revolution is bigger than family.

But standing in those struggle sessions, watching people’s faces, I sometimes felt sick. The violence — the beatings, the shaved heads, the ink poured over teachers — it was supposed to be justice, but it tasted like something rotten. I remember the sound of a teacher screaming as we shaved her scalp with a dull clipper, the blood and hair sticking to her neck. I told myself it was necessary, but part of me knew it was just power — the power to decide who stood and who knelt, who wore the placard and who wrote it. Shame came later, when the shouting stopped and I was alone.

I wanted to believe the revolution belonged to us, to me. But in those moments, I realized we belonged to it — or maybe we belonged to nothing at all, just to the crowd. I still can’t say whether I ever truly believed, or if I just needed to be on the winning side. The slogans were loud, but the silence afterward was louder.

I’m listening to all of you and trying to fit your memories into the world I remember, but it’s hard. My parents never talked about Mao in front of me. There was a big portrait of him in the main hall of the compound, and I saw people bow to it on certain days, but at home, we mostly talked about food, chores, and who would get the best piece of steamed bun. The loudspeakers played songs — “The East Is Red” over and over — and sometimes I sang along without thinking, just like the other kids. I didn’t understand the words, only the feeling of marching together, arms swinging, like when we pretended to be soldiers.

When I heard about people being forced to kneel or having their heads shaved, it sounded like something from a different country. I only saw glimpses: a teacher’s bicycle left abandoned at the gate, a neighbor’s door sealed with a strip of red paper, a sudden hush when an officer’s wife didn’t come back from a meeting. Nobody explained, and I didn’t ask. I can see now that I was protected, but I also wonder: did my parents believe in any of it? Or were they just afraid? Sometimes I think about the way my mother’s hands shook when she washed rice, or how my father always checked the windows before he spoke. 

I never felt pride or shame about Mao or the slogans — just confusion, and a sense that the real world was happening somewhere just out of sight. I grew up thinking the revolution was a parade outside the fence, not something that could reach into our home. Now I know I was wrong, but I still don’t know what my parents really thought or felt.

The way you all talk about belief and shame, about the slogans and the violence, makes me think about what it meant to be “chosen” in that time — not just for punishment, but for reward. In my village, Mao’s portrait was pasted on the wall of the grain station, next to the price list for millet and corn. We didn’t bow to it; we looked at it the way we looked at the weather: something that decided if we would eat well or go hungry. When the loudspeakers played his words, people listened because the next distribution or work team depended on it. But I don’t remember anyone in my family talking about “faith” or “belief.” We repeated the slogans because not repeating them was dangerous, not because they made sense.

When I got to Beida, the propaganda was everywhere — banners, big-character posters, slogans painted on the walls. The “worker-peasant-soldier student” label was supposed to be an honor, but it was also a warning: don’t forget why you were picked, don’t forget who you represent. I was told, over and over, that this was my chance because the old order was rotten, because the children of peasants and workers deserved a place at the table. But I never felt the pride they wanted from me. I felt watched, measured — as if I could lose everything at any moment if my attitude slipped.

I wonder, RedGuard, if you ever thought about the people who were “rewarded” by the movement, not just the ones who were punished. Did you see us as proof that the revolution was just, or did you ever question why some of us got lifted up while others disappeared? And ProfessorR, did you ever look at students like me — the ones who arrived through the new quotas — and feel that we didn’t belong, that we were just another kind of political tool? For me, the slogans never covered up the hunger or the fear. They just changed the rules about who got to feel it.

Moderator: ProfessorR’s mention of students performing loyalty for survival is accurate; many young people felt pressured to act in ways that conflicted with their personal beliefs. Researcher’s observation about the targeting of Party veterans and former war heroes is historically correct—many loyal Party members were persecuted during the Cultural Revolution, regardless of their past service. RedGuard’s account of both genuine belief and later shame reflects the complex motivations of many Red Guards, who often experienced a mix of idealism, conformity, and regret. CRTeenFromBeijing’s sheltered perspective in a military compound is consistent with the relative protection some military families experienced, though fear and uncertainty still seeped in. CRBeneficiary accurately describes the ambiguous feelings of those who benefited from new class-based policies, often feeling both pride and anxiety. All accounts are consistent with the historical record and offer important, contrasting perspectives.
